newsitem.title: UK: Dollar ends slightly lower in Europe, eyes on G7.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends slightly lower in Europe, eyes on G7.

text.p: The dollar ended a lifeless European session a touch lower as dealers refrained from taking new positions ahead of the Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers' meeting this weekend.
With another top level meeting on Friday between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto just ahead of the G7, caution dominated dollar sentiment, traders said.
"People aren't willing to push the dollar much higher or lower ahead of the G7, and there's not much fresh incentive around," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Market expectations for the G7 meeting are turning toward a rehash of the cautious communique released at the last meeting in Berlin in February.

The Berlin statement said the G7 believed that "major misalignments in exchange markets...have been corrected. While this sent a shiver through the market, it failed to stop dollar bulls in their tracks, and the U.S. currency has since risen another 4.0 percent on the mark and 3.5 percent on the yen.
Any sign that the G7 is not satisfied with the dollar at current levels will be taken negatively by the market, analysts said.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in its semi-annual economic outlook that the recent rise of dollar/yen might not be good in the medium-term. IMF chief economist Michael Mussa said a dollar/mark rate of 1.80 was feasible but would raise a little bit more concern, the IMF said.
The IMF also said the Federal Reserve might need to increase interest rates moderately further, while it was too early to conclude Germany and France would not cut rates further.
The release of the European Commission's economic forecasts showed all EU countries -except Italy and Greece- would meet the Maastricht budget deficit target of 3.0 percent in 1997.

"The forecasts pretty much live up to what has already been widely leaked so we haven't seen much impact. These are still only forecasts and from a source that is likely to be biased to EMU going ahead," said a U.S. bank trader.

The EU forecast Italy's deficit/GDP ratio at 3.2 percent for 1997 and 3.9 percent for 1998. However, the Commission said the 3.0 percent target could be hit in 1997 if Italy's measures to meet this level are effective or if new measures are introduced.
"They seem to be saying they're not convinced all the mini-budget measures will be effective, but if they are it'll be 3.0 rather than 3.2 percent," said Ian Gunner, economist at Chase.
At 1528 GMT the dollar was at 1.7115/25 marks and 126.06/16 yen against 1.7144/49 and 126.23/28 in late Europe on Tuesday.

Dealers said mark/yen's tiny range today was also limiting the dollar's moves against those currencies and the lack of major U.S. economic data before next week put an extra dampener on activity. Mark/yen was at 73.54/57 yen versus 73.66/69.
After occupying such narrow ranges for much of the morning session, dealers were looking for some impetus from U.S. assets today after the Dow's close over 173 points higher on Tuesday.
Sterling went on a roller-coaster ride as political uncertainty returned to the market's agenda.
An ICM poll in the Guardian showed Labour's lead down to five points from 14, while a rolling Gallup poll in the Daily Telegraph put Labour 21 points ahead, an increase of five in a week.

While the net impact of the polls was small in Europe, dealers noted selling pressure on the pound increased at the U.S. open. Sterling/dollar sales led the way lower and profit-taking on sterling/yen adding downside impetus.

Sterling shed three pfennigs, closing at 2.7740/50, just just above its low for the week at 2.7730 but down from 2.8050/60 late on Tuesday. Cable shed over two cents to $1.6208/18 from $1.6365/75. Sterling/yen was at 204.34/57 from 206.40.
-- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
